Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "we need a prompt for a visitor-facing text for the North Quay Museum in Alderwick, for the small local-history exhibit “Across Mill Creek: the landing and its neighborhood.” The gallery room used to be the map room. This is an exhibit about the old Mill Creek landing and the people and places around it, not a general history of Alderwick or a full account of ferry transport. The readers will be local visitors and people who don’t already know the site. Keep the language clear enough to read while standing in the gallery. Please make a draft of about 450–600 words, with a title and a short opening, then three numbered sections, and a few short image captions at the end. It should feel like an exhibit text, not a brochure or an academic paper. Send the draft to Leonie, not Ellis; the routing field should read exactly “Leonie not Ellis.”

Here are the notes from the museum’s source file, not all of them are equally certain so please keep the difference clear. A municipal ledger records that ferry service began in 1912 and says it was operated by the landing association, not the city. The ledger gives no route map. An insurance plan from 1949 shows the landing, a shed, and stairs on the east bank, but doesn’t give a ferry schedule. A local newspaper notice says passenger service stopped in 1964. The notice does not say whether freight service continued, so we don’t know that from this source. A public works log records that a retaining wall was built along Mill Creek in 1971 and the stairs were removed. The log does not give a demolition date for the shed. Don’t make one up. There are photographs with 1936 handwritten on the back by the donor; the date hasn’t been independently checked. They can be called photographs dated 1936 by the donor, but don’t present that date as proven. The museum has no route map in the file, even though the ledger refers to a route. Please don’t draw or describe a specific route that isn’t documented.

Interview excerpts are part of the material and should appear in the exhibit text as quotes, not be rewritten as statements from the museum. Ada Lorne was born in 1940 and says she remembers going to the landing as a child. Her excerpt: “The bell carried across the water before you could see the boat. On Saturdays my mother sent me ahead to wait, and I watched people bring baskets down the stairs.” Keep the recollection in Ada’s voice. It is her memory of the place, not proof that every Saturday was the same or a record of a ferry schedule. Ben Ives worked at a repair shop near the creek from 1958 to 1967. His excerpt: “We could hear the work at the landing from the shop, especially when they were fixing a rail. I never worked on the ferry itself.” Don’t imply Ben was a ferryman or did repairs on the boat. He is talking about what he heard from the nearby shop.

The third interview is with Salma Ortiz, who moved to Alderwick in 1982. Her excerpt is: “By then the stairs were gone, but people still used the bank as a place to meet. If someone said ‘down by the old landing,’ everyone knew where they meant.” This is her account of what she saw and heard after moving to town, not direct evidence about the ferry’s working years. Please keep that distinction, and don’t turn the line into a claim that the landing itself was still operating. The quotes above are the supplied excerpts. Use them as given, with the names attached. The museum wants visitors to see the difference between records, photographs, and personal memories without making the text sound doubtful about everything.

A possible way to organize the sections is the record of the landing and its operation, remembered life around it, and what changed along the creek. Use the numbered sections if that structure works, but the text should stay connected rather than read like a stack of disconnected facts. Explain that the landing association, rather than the city, operated the service according to the ledger. Mention the 1949 plan’s landing, shed, and east-bank stairs, then the later evidence about service ending and the wall and stairs. Be careful not to imply that the 1971 work log dates the shed’s removal. Include a brief reference to the donor-dated photographs only with the qualification in the notes. The exhibit is focused on the landing and neighborhood; don’t add a broad town timeline, invented residents, additional historical events, or claims about why the ferry stopped.

For the short opening, orient a visitor to Mill Creek and the landing, using only what is in these notes. The three numbered sections can cover the documentary record, the lived memories in the interviews, and the later physical changes, while allowing the material to connect naturally. The captions should be short and must not claim that a particular supplied image shows a particular person, event, or structure unless the notes establish it. The photographs are only described in this file as photographs with 1936 written on their backs by the donor, so don’t assign them a more precise subject. No image inventory or additional caption facts have been supplied. Don’t fill the gaps with plausible details; leave out what cannot be supported rather than guessing.

Please make the result usable as a draft for the exhibit, with the source limits respected but without putting source-file commentary or instructions to the writer into the visitor-facing text. The records and interview excerpts should be woven into the text in a natural way, and the quotations should remain clearly attributed. Keep the language direct and readable, not overly solemn. The closing part of the text can point to the recorded changes at the creek and the continuing place-name in Salma’s recollection, but it must not announce a museum conclusion or claim a current use beyond what she says. Include no proposed event, opening date, approval, or recommendation. The task here is to draft the exhibit text from the supplied material, not to add research or describe an outcome.", "output": "Create a visitor-facing draft of about 450–600 words for the North Quay Museum in Alderwick’s small local-history exhibit, “Across Mill Creek: the landing and its neighborhood.” The gallery room was formerly the map room. Focus on the old Mill Creek landing and the people and places around it, rather than a general history of Alderwick or ferry transport. Write for local visitors and people unfamiliar with the site. Use clear language suitable for reading while standing in a gallery; the style should feel like an exhibit text, not a brochure or academic paper.

**Format and recipient**

Include a title, a short opening, three numbered sections, and a few short image captions at the end. Keep the sections connected rather than presenting a stack of unrelated facts. Send the draft to Leonie, not Ellis; the routing field should read exactly “Leonie not Ellis.”

**Source notes**

Use the records with their stated limits:

- A municipal ledger records that ferry service began in 1912 and was operated by the landing association, not the city. The ledger includes no route map.
- A 1949 insurance plan shows the landing, a shed, and stairs on the east bank. It gives no ferry schedule.
- A local newspaper notice says passenger service stopped in 1964. It does not say whether freight service continued.
- A public works log records that a retaining wall was built along Mill Creek in 1971 and the stairs were removed. The log does not give a demolition date for the shed.
- Photographs have “1936” handwritten on their backs by the donor. That date has not been independently checked. Refer to them only as photographs dated 1936 by the donor, not as definitively dated images.

Do not supply an undocumented route, a reason the ferry stopped, a shed demolition date, or other unsupported details. No route map is in the file, despite the ledger’s reference to a route.

**Interview excerpts**

Use the supplied excerpts as quotes, with the speakers’ names attached. Do not rewrite them as statements by the museum.

Ada Lorne was born in 1940 and recalls visiting the landing as a child: “The bell carried across the water before you could see the boat. On Saturdays my mother sent me ahead to wait, and I watched people bring baskets down the stairs.” Present this as Ada’s memory, not as proof that every Saturday followed the same pattern or as a ferry schedule.

Ben Ives worked at a repair shop near the creek from 1958 to 1967: “We could hear the work at the landing from the shop, especially when they were fixing a rail. I never worked on the ferry itself.” Do not imply that Ben was a ferryman or repaired the boat; he describes what he heard from the nearby shop.

Salma Ortiz moved to Alderwick in 1982: “By then the stairs were gone, but people still used the bank as a place to meet. If someone said ‘down by the old landing,’ everyone knew where they meant.” This is her account of what she saw and heard after moving to town, not direct evidence about the ferry’s working years. Do not imply that the landing was still operating. The museum wants visitors to understand the differences between records, photographs, and personal memories without making the text sound doubtful about everything.

**Suggested structure and limits**

The numbered sections may cover the documentary record and operation of the landing, remembered life around it, and later changes along the creek. Explain that the ledger identifies the landing association, rather than the city, as the operator. Refer to the 1949 plan’s landing, shed, and east-bank stairs, then to the later evidence about passenger service and the retaining wall and stairs. Do not suggest that the 1971 work log dates the shed’s removal. Include a brief, qualified reference to the donor-dated photographs.

Use the opening to orient visitors to Mill Creek and the landing, based only on the supplied information. Captions must be short and must not assign a specific subject, person, event, or structure to an image unless the notes establish it. The file gives no more precise description of the photographs, and no image inventory or additional caption facts are supplied; do not guess.

Keep the text direct, readable, and not overly solemn. Weave in the records and attributed quotations naturally. The closing may refer to the recorded changes at the creek and the continuing place-name in Salma’s recollection, but must not announce a museum conclusion or claim a current use beyond what she says. Do not add a broad town timeline, invented residents or events, proposed event, opening date, approval, recommendation, or unsupported present-day claims. Draft the exhibit text from the supplied material; do not add research or describe an outcome."}]
